templates.title: Delivery promise kept, on the customer's local date
templates.subtopic: time zones, order-level rollups before grouping, outer joins

sections.scenario: An online marketplace shows every order a promised delivery date, and customers judge the promise by the calendar at their own address: a parcel handed over at 8 p.m. in Los Angeles is on time for a customer promised that day, even though it is already the next day in UTC. Carrier scans are recorded as UTC instants. The delivery-experience team wants a daily scorecard of promises kept, per {{group_col}}.
sections.problem: Write one PostgreSQL query that returns, for every (promised_date, {{group_col}}) that has orders: promised_date, {{group_col}}, orders, on_time, late, undelivered, on_time_pct = ROUND(100.0 * on_time / orders, 1) and max_days_late (the largest number of days a late order arrived after its promised date, NULL when the group has no late order). An order is on time when it is delivered and the local date of its delivery, in the order's dest_tz, is on or before promised_date; late when it is delivered after that date; undelivered otherwise. {{package_rule}} {{scan_rule}} Order by promised_date, {{group_col}}.
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). Every order appears in exactly one of the three outcomes, so on_time + late + undelivered = orders. The sample has {{n_orders}} orders; production has millions of orders a day across many fulfilment centres and destination time zones.
sections.assumptions: Hypothetical schema, identifiers, carriers and promises. dest_tz is a valid IANA time zone name. Every promised date in the sample is already in the past, so an order with no delivery by now is not going to change the scorecard by arriving early.
sections.criteria: Converts each delivery to the destination's local date before comparing; judges an order by its last package; first DELIVERED scan per package; attempts are not deliveries; keeps unshipped and undelivered orders in the denominator via LEFT JOINs; on-or-before comparison; exact rounding and NULL max_days_late; deterministic ordering.

clarifications.q: Which date decides on time: UTC or local?
clarifications.a: The destination's local date. Convert the delivery instant with AT TIME ZONE dest_tz, then take the date.

clarifications.q: When is a multi-package order delivered?
clarifications.a: When its last package is delivered. Until then the customer does not have the order.

clarifications.q: Is a delivery on the promised date itself on time?
clarifications.a: Yes. On or before the promised local date is on time.

clarifications.q: Does an undelivered order count in the percentage?
clarifications.a: Yes. It is in orders (the denominator) and not in on_time.

clarifications.q: What does max_days_late measure?
clarifications.a: Local delivery date minus promised date, in whole days, over late orders only.

hints: Bring everything to one row per order before grouping: the number of packages, the number delivered, and the latest local delivery date.
(delivered_at AT TIME ZONE dest_tz)::date turns a timestamptz into the local calendar date at the destination; DST is handled by the zone name.
Reduce scans to one delivery time per package first (MIN(scanned_at) over DELIVERED), then LEFT JOIN from orders so nothing disappears.
followups: The scorecard runs hourly while parcels are still arriving. How do you keep "undelivered" from being read as "late" for promises that are still in the future?
A destination's dest_tz is missing for 0.5% of orders. What do you do with them, and how do you make sure the percentage is not quietly biased?
At hundreds of millions of scans a day, which table do you pre-aggregate, at what grain, and how do late scans (devices that upload a day later) correct it?
The business now wants promises judged per package for split shipments, and per order for the customer view. How do you model both without double-counting?

rules.ask: Your date is taken from a timestamptz. In which time zone, and what happens to a parcel delivered at 21:00 in Los Angeles?
Which orders have no row on the other side of that join, and where do they end up in your counts?
An order shipped as three packages; two arrived early and one arrived two days late. What did the customer experience, and what does your query say?
A package has two DELIVERED scans a day apart because a device re-synced. Which one is the delivery?

templates.title: Package scan silences
templates.subtopic: LEAD over ordered events, bounded sequences, per-group arg-max

sections.scenario: A parcel moving through a delivery network is scanned at every hand-off: picked up, arrived at and departed from sort centres and delivery stations, out for delivery, delivered. A long stretch with no scan is how lost or stuck parcels show up first. The network-operations team wants a list of packages whose longest silence reached {{min_hours}} hours, with the facility where each one went quiet. The seller's label is created before the carrier has the parcel, and that wait is the seller's, not the network's.
sections.problem: Write one PostgreSQL query against package_scans that returns one row per package whose longest silence is at least {{min_hours}} hours: package_id, delivered (whether the package has a DELIVERED scan), gap_started_at (the scanned_at of the scan before the silence), facility_id (that scan's facility) and gap_hours = ROUND(seconds / 3600, 2). A package's scans are ordered by (scanned_at, scan_id). The scans that count run from its first carrier scan (any scan_type other than LABEL_CREATED) up to and including its first DELIVERED scan, and a silence is the time between two consecutive counted scans. {{end_rule}} If two silences of one package tie for the longest, report the earlier. Order by the silence's exact length descending, then package_id. The report's as_of is {{as_of}}.
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). The threshold is inclusive: exactly {{min_hours}} hours qualifies. The sample has {{n_scans}} scans for {{n_packages}} packages; production has billions of scans a month.
sections.assumptions: Hypothetical facilities, scan types and timings. scan_id is unique and breaks ties between scans recorded at the same second. All timestamps are UTC instants.
sections.criteria: Orders scans by (scanned_at, scan_id); starts at the first carrier scan and stops at the first DELIVERED scan; LEAD (or equivalent) over the bounded sequence; reports the facility before the silence; earliest of equal longest silences; at the Very Hard level, the open silence to as_of for undelivered packages and no row for label-only packages; inclusive threshold; deterministic ordering.

clarifications.q: Does the wait between LABEL_CREATED and pickup count?
clarifications.a: No. Until the first carrier scan the seller still has the parcel.

clarifications.q: What about scans after delivery, such as a return pickup?
clarifications.a: They are ignored: counting stops at the first DELIVERED scan.

clarifications.q: Which facility do I report?
clarifications.a: The facility of the scan before the silence: that is where the parcel went quiet.

clarifications.q: Two scans have the same timestamp. Which comes first?
clarifications.a: The smaller scan_id. Their silence is zero.

clarifications.q: Is a silence of exactly {{min_hours}} hours reported?
clarifications.a: Yes. The threshold is inclusive.

hints: Number each package's scans with ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY package_id ORDER BY scanned_at, scan_id), then find the first carrier scan and the first DELIVERED scan per package as row numbers.
Keep the rows between those two bounds; LEAD(scanned_at) over the kept rows gives the end of each silence.
Pick each package's longest silence with DISTINCT ON (package_id) … ORDER BY package_id, gap DESC, rn.
followups: Operations wants this alert within an hour of a parcel going quiet, not in a nightly batch. What state do you keep per package, and when does the alert fire?
Some facilities upload scans in batches every few hours. How do you tell a stuck parcel from a facility whose scanners are offline?
Thresholds differ: a silence of 6 hours on an out-for-delivery van is alarming, 30 hours on a long linehaul is normal. How would you model expected silences per leg?
At billions of scans, how would you partition and cluster package_scans so this query reads only recent packages?

rules.ask: Your window runs over all of a package's scans. What does it do with the label-to-pickup wait and with a return pickup three days after delivery?
That measures the whole journey. Which parcel has a 40-hour journey with no silence over 10 hours, and which has a 20-hour journey with one 15-hour silence?
How do you find "the next scan" with a self-join when two scans share a timestamp, and what does it cost on a package with 40 scans?

when: partition by package_id order by scanned_at
rules.ask: Two scans have the same scanned_at. Is your order deterministic, and which facility do you report?

templates.title: Shared cloud cost split by tagged usage, to the cent
templates.subtopic: proportional allocation, largest-remainder rounding, window functions

sections.scenario: A company runs on a public cloud and reads its bill from a cost and usage report: one line item per account, usage day, service and charge type, with the team's cost-allocation tag where the resource was tagged. Some cost can never be tagged to one team (shared networking, monitoring, data transfer). Finance charges that shared cost back to teams in proportion to what each team used, and every cent of the pool must land on exactly one team.
sections.problem: Write one PostgreSQL query on cur_line_items that returns one row per (account_id, team): direct_cents (the team's tagged usage), allocated_cents (its share of untagged usage) and total_cents = direct_cents + allocated_cents. Within each (account_id, usage_date), the untagged usage cost is the pool P, and each team with tagged usage that day, with tagged cost t out of the day's tagged total T, gets floor(P * t / T) cents; the cents still left over go one each to the teams with the largest remainders (P * t) mod T, ties broken by team name ascending. {{period_rule}} {{type_rule}} {{tag_rule}} Order by account_id, team.
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). Integer arithmetic only: no floating point, no rounding of fractions of a cent. For every pool, the allocated cents add up to exactly P. The sample has {{n_items}} line items; a large organisation's report has hundreds of millions of rows a month.
sections.assumptions: Hypothetical accounts, teams, services and amounts. Real reports carry costs as decimals with more precision; this extract has been rounded to whole cents. Treating tag values as case-insensitive is this exercise's business rule, not a property of any provider's tags.
sections.criteria: Pools per (account, usage day); usage lines only; exact integer floor and remainder; leftover cents by largest remainder with team-name tie-break; allocations sum to the pool; daily results added up per team; at the Very Hard level, normalised tags, empty tags as untagged and an 'unallocated' row for pools with no tagged usage; deterministic ordering.

clarifications.q: Is the split per day or over the whole period?
clarifications.a: Per (account_id, usage_date). Each day's pool follows that day's tagged usage; then add the days up.

clarifications.q: Does a team with no tagged usage on a day get any of that day's pool?
clarifications.a: No. Only teams with tagged usage that day share it.

clarifications.q: Can I use ROUND on each share?
clarifications.a: No. Independently rounded shares need not add up to the pool. Floor, then hand out the leftover cents by largest remainder.

clarifications.q: Two teams have the same remainder and there is one cent left. Who gets it?
clarifications.a: The team whose name sorts first.

clarifications.q: Does one account's pool ever go to another account's teams?
clarifications.a: Never. Pools are per account.

hints: Build two aggregates per (account_id, usage_date): tagged cost per team, and the untagged pool. Join the pool onto the teams.

With integers, P * t / T is floor division and P * t % T the remainder (both are non-negative here). In PostgreSQL SUM(bigint) returns numeric, so cast the sums back with ::bigint first. SUM(t) OVER (PARTITION BY account_id, usage_date) gives T.
Leftover cents = P − SUM(floor) over the pool. Rank teams by (remainder DESC, team) with ROW_NUMBER(); the first leftover of them get one more cent.
followups: Finance asks why the allocation for one team changed after the month closed. Which late-arriving line items change a past day's allocation, and how do you make the report reproducible?
Proportional to cost penalises teams on expensive instance types for shared network traffic they did not cause. What other drivers could you allocate by, and what data would each need?
At hundreds of millions of line items a month, which intermediate tables would you materialise, and at what grain?
Some shared cost belongs to a platform team that itself serves other teams. How would you allocate in two stages without creating a cycle?

rules.ask: Three teams with equal usage share a pool of 100 cents. What does your rounding give each, and where did the missing cent go?
A team used nothing on Monday and a lot on Tuesday. Should it carry part of Monday's shared cost?
Which function do you rank remainders with, and what happens to the leftover cents when two teams tie under it?
What does your query do with a tag value of ' Checkout' or an empty string?

templates.title: Usage above a capacity commitment
templates.subtopic: interval events, half-open intervals, per-key integration

sections.scenario: A cloud customer pays in advance for a fixed amount of capacity in an instance family for a period: a commitment. Usage covered by the commitment costs nothing extra; anything running above it at a given moment is billed at the on-demand rate. The FinOps team wants to know, from a year or more of instance start and stop records, how much usage ran above the commitments, so it can decide whether to commit to more.
sections.problem: Implement on_demand_unit_seconds(usages, commitments). Each usage is (start_s, end_s, family, units): an instance of that family running during the half-open interval [start_s, end_s). Each commitment is (start_s, end_s, family, units): capacity paid for during [start_s, end_s). At any moment t, used_f(t) is the sum of units of usages of family f running at t, and committed_f(t) the sum of units of commitments of f active at t. Return a dict mapping every family that appears in usages to the integer ∫ max(0, used_f(t) − committed_f(t)) dt in unit-seconds (0 if nothing ran above the commitment; a usage with start_s == end_s runs for no time but still puts its family in the result). Families that appear only in commitments are not in the result. {{family_rule}} {{unit_rule}}
sections.constraints: Up to 200 000 usages over several years of per-second timestamps, and up to a few hundred commitments; 0 ≤ start_s ≤ end_s. Expected: O((n + c) log(n + c)). A loop over every second, or rescanning every usage for every interval, is too slow.
sections.assumptions: Hypothetical families, sizes and commitments. Real cloud commitment discounts (capacity reservations, savings plans) have their own documented matching and billing rules; this exercise uses a simplified rule on purpose. Unused commitment at one moment is not carried to another.
sections.criteria: Half-open intervals; per-family independence; positive part only (no banking); every usage family in the result, zero-length included; commitments of unused families excluded; overlapping commitments add up and units weigh both sides; O(n log n) via a sorted sweep with all changes at a time applied before integrating.

clarifications.q: An instance stops at second 100 and another starts at second 100. Do they overlap?
clarifications.a: No. Intervals are half-open, [start, end).

clarifications.q: If the commitment is 3 units and 1 unit is running, is the result negative?
clarifications.a: No. Only usage above the commitment counts; spare commitment is wasted, never credited.

clarifications.q: Does a commitment for one family cover another family's usage?
clarifications.a: No. Families are independent.

clarifications.q: Do I report a family whose usage was all covered?
clarifications.a: Yes, with 0. Every family in usages is in the result.

hints: Turn every interval into two events: +units at its start and −units at its end (commitments with the opposite sign). Only the times where something changes matter.
Sort the event times per family and walk them: between two consecutive times, used − committed is constant, so its positive part times the gap is the on-demand amount for that stretch.
Apply every change at a time before integrating the next stretch; then the order of events at the same time does not matter.
followups: The FinOps team asks: what commitment level C would have minimised cost over last year, given an on-demand price and a commitment price per unit-second? Use your sweep to answer it.
Usage records arrive as an unbounded stream, partitioned across 50 workers. How do you compute the same number per hour, and what must reach one place?
A commitment may cover several families at a discount ratio (a larger family consumes it faster). How does your state change?
The usage list has 2 billion rows for the whole organisation. Which parts of the sweep would you do in SQL, and which can you not?

rules.ask: The timing test spans four years. How many iterations is that per family, and how much memory does an array per second need?
Two events share a timestamp: one instance stops and another starts. Does the order you process them in change your answer?
How much memory does your solution hold at once, and could you stream families one at a time?
What query does that structure answer that a single sorted sweep does not need here?

templates.title: Dock doors for inbound trailers
templates.subtopic: event simulation, priority queues, deterministic tie-breaks

sections.scenario: A fulfilment centre receives inventory from trailers that back into numbered dock doors. Trailers that arrive while every door is busy wait in the yard. Planners want to replay a day (or a peak season) of arrivals under a simple, fixed rule to see when each trailer would start unloading and at which door, before they change the rule or add doors.
sections.problem: Implement assign_doors(trailers, doors). Each trailer is (arrival_min, trailer_id, unload_min, priority); doors are numbered 1..doors and all free at the start. Whenever at least one door is free and at least one trailer has arrived and is waiting, the first waiting trailer takes the lowest-numbered free door and starts unloading at that minute; its door is busy during [start, start + unload_min) and free again at start + unload_min. The first waiting trailer is the one with the smallest priority, then the earliest arrival_min, then the smallest trailer_id. A door that frees at minute t can be taken at t, including by a trailer arriving at t, and before choosing at minute t every trailer that has arrived by t is in the yard. Return a dict mapping each trailer_id to (door, start_min). {{order_rule}} {{priority_rule}}
sections.constraints: Up to 200 000 trailers and a few hundred doors; minutes are non-negative integers, unload_min ≥ 1, trailer ids are unique. At peak the yard holds tens of thousands of trailers. Expected: O(n log n).
sections.assumptions: Hypothetical arrivals, unload times and priorities. Real yard and dock scheduling uses appointments, door types and labour plans; this replay deliberately has one fixed rule.
sections.criteria: A door freed at t is usable at t; arrivals at t join before assigning; lowest free door; yard order (priority, arrival, trailer_id); no preemption; input sorted by the candidate; time jumps between events; O(n log n) with heaps for free doors, busy doors and the yard.

clarifications.q: A door frees at minute 40 and a trailer arrives at minute 40. Can it use that door?
clarifications.a: Yes, at minute 40.

clarifications.q: Two doors are free. Which one does the trailer take?
clarifications.a: The lowest-numbered.

clarifications.q: Can an urgent trailer stop an unload in progress?
clarifications.a: No. It waits for the next free door, and then goes ahead of less urgent trailers.

clarifications.q: How are trailer_id values compared?
clarifications.a: As strings, in the usual ascending order.

clarifications.q: Is the input sorted?
clarifications.a: Do not rely on it; sort it yourself.

hints: Keep three heaps: free door numbers, busy doors keyed by the minute they free up, and the yard keyed by (priority, arrival_min, trailer_id).
Jump time, never step it: if the yard is empty, jump to the next arrival; if it is not empty and no door is free, jump to the next door to free up.
At each jump, first free the doors and admit the arrivals up to that minute, then assign while both a door and a trailer are available.
followups: Planners want the average and the 95th-percentile yard wait per priority. What do you add, and what does the 95th percentile cost to compute exactly?
Some doors can only take refrigerated trailers. How do the heaps change when a trailer can only use some doors?
Low-priority trailers can now wait forever behind a stream of urgent ones. Propose an aging rule and say how it changes your data structures.
Replay a full peak season for 900 sites, each independently. How would you run it, and what would you store for analysis?

rules.ask: How long does the yard get in the timing test, and what does finding the next trailer cost per assignment in your structure?
How many minutes does the timing test span, and how many of them change anything?
What exactly is your yard heap keyed on, and what happens when two trailers tie on priority and arrival?
With 300 doors and 200 000 trailers, how many door checks is that, and how would a heap of free doors change it?

templates.title: Cheapest shipment plan for a multi-item order
templates.subtopic: subset DP over bitmasks, split shipments

sections.scenario: A customer buys several different items in one marketplace order. Several fulfilment centres each stock some of those items. Shipping a package from a centre costs a fixed package cost (picking, packing, the box and the carrier's base charge) plus a per-item cost that depends on the item and on how far that centre is from the customer. The order may be split into several packages from different centres. Before the order is released to the centres, a routing step must choose the cheapest way to ship it.
sections.problem: Implement plan_shipments(items, centres, max_items=None). items is a list of distinct SKUs, one unit each. centres is a list of (centre_id, package_cost, units), where units maps each SKU the centre can ship to its per-item cost. A plan puts every item in exactly one package. A package comes from one centre, holds only items that centre stocks, and costs package_cost plus the per-item costs of its items. A centre may send more than one package, and each one pays the package cost. Return (total_cost, packages) for the cheapest plan. If two plans cost the same, return the one with fewer packages. An empty order returns (0, 0). If an item is stocked by no centre, return None. {{stock_rule}} {{box_rule}}
sections.constraints: Up to 13 items in an order and 40 centres. All costs are non-negative integers in cents, below 10 000. A centre's units may list SKUs that are not in this order. Something close to O(m · 2ⁿ + 3ⁿ) is expected for n items and m centres. Trying every assignment of items to centres is not fast enough.
sections.assumptions: All costs are hypothetical. Every centre that lists a SKU has the one unit this order needs. Delivery speed is the same from every centre in this exercise, so only cost matters.
sections.criteria: Correct (cost, packages) with fewest packages on cost ties; None for an item no centre stocks and (0, 0) for an empty order; packages limited to items their centre stocks; box limit applied per package, with several packages from one centre allowed; a subset DP that precomputes the cheapest single package per subset and fixes the lowest item to avoid counting a partition twice; integer arithmetic; a clear complexity argument; sensible answers on capacity, delivery dates and large orders.

clarifications.q: Can one centre send two packages?
clarifications.a: Yes, and each pays the package cost. Without a box limit that is never cheaper than one package, but with max_items it can be necessary.

clarifications.q: Does a centre's dict say how many units it has?
clarifications.a: No. Listing a SKU means the centre can ship the one unit this order needs.

clarifications.q: If two plans cost the same, which do I return?
clarifications.a: The one with fewer packages. The answer is just the pair (cost, packages), so it is unique even when several plans tie.

clarifications.q: Does the order of items or centres matter?
clarifications.a: No. The answer does not depend on either order.

clarifications.q: What do I return for an order with no items?
clarifications.a: (0, 0).

hints: With 13 items there are 8 192 subsets. For each subset, what is the cheapest single package that could carry exactly those items?
Let best[mask] be the cheapest way to ship the items in mask. The lowest item in mask is in some package. Try every package that contains it, and add best of the items that remain.
Compare (cost, packages) pairs as tuples, or pack them into one integer so that a single comparison orders both.
followups: Your plan is the cheapest, but it splits an order into four boxes and customers prefer fewer. How would you add a per-package penalty or a hard limit on packages, and what changes in your DP?
Centres have limited units, and thousands of orders are planned in the same minute. Why is planning each order on its own no longer optimal, and what would you do instead?
Different centres give different delivery dates. How do you find the cheapest plan that still meets the date promised to the customer?
Orders with 40 items appear, and the subset DP is out of reach. What would you do, and how would you measure how far from optimal your plans are?

rules.ask: Give an order where shipping each item from its cheapest centre is not the cheapest plan. What does the package cost do to a per-item greedy choice?
How many assignments are there with 13 items and 40 centres, and how long would that take?
Choosing the set of centres first works without a box limit. What breaks when max_items is set, and how large is 2^m with 40 centres?
How many states does your memo hold, and how many transitions does each state try? Write the total.
You use floating-point infinity next to integer cents. Where could a float sneak into the total, and how would you keep the answer exact?

templates.title: Earliest arrival through scheduled linehauls
templates.subtopic: time-dependent shortest paths, schedules and binary search

sections.scenario: A package becomes ready to leave a fulfilment centre at a known minute. It moves through sort centres to the delivery station that serves the customer, on scheduled linehaul trucks. Each lane between two nodes has departures at fixed minutes, and each departure has its own transit time. At every sort centre the package needs some handling time before it can leave again. The delivery date shown to the customer depends on the earliest minute the package can reach the delivery station, so this calculation runs for every package.
sections.problem: Implement earliest_arrival(lanes, handling, origin, dest, ready, daily=False). lanes is a list of (from_node, to_node, departures), and departures is a list of (depart_minute, transit_minutes). A package at a node can take a departure if depart_minute is at or after the minute the package is ready at that node. At origin it is ready at ready. At any other node it is ready at its arrival minute plus handling.get(node, 0). A departure arrives at depart_minute + transit_minutes. Return the earliest minute the package can arrive at dest, with no handling added there, or None if no sequence of departures reaches it. If origin == dest, return ready. {{schedule_rule}} {{daily_rule}}
sections.constraints: Up to 5 000 nodes, 40 000 lanes and 20 departures per lane. Every transit time is at least 1 minute. Departures are not sorted, and two lanes may join the same pair of nodes. Something close to O(D log D + L log N) is expected, for D departures, L lanes and N nodes.
sections.assumptions: The network, schedules and handling times are hypothetical. Trucks have unlimited room. A package may wait at any node for as long as it needs. Handling time at a node is the same for every package.
sections.criteria: Inclusive departure rule; handling only at intermediate nodes; None when unreachable and ready when origin equals destination; the earliest arrival over all catchable departures, not just the next one; Dijkstra on arrival time, justified by waiting being allowed; sorted departures with suffix minima and binary search; correct day arithmetic for daily schedules and transits longer than a day; a credible answer on capacity, uncertainty and recomputation.

clarifications.q: Can the package take a departure at exactly the minute it becomes ready?
clarifications.a: Yes. A departure can be taken when depart_minute is greater than or equal to the ready minute.

clarifications.q: Is handling time added at the origin or at the destination?
clarifications.a: No. At the origin the package is ready at ready, and the answer is the arrival minute at the destination.

clarifications.q: Are a lane's departures sorted?
clarifications.a: No, and two departures may leave at the same minute.

clarifications.q: Can two lanes join the same two nodes?
clarifications.a: Yes, for example two carriers. Consider both.

clarifications.q: Is arriving earlier at a sort centre always at least as good as arriving later?
clarifications.a: Yes, because the package can wait. That property is what makes an efficient algorithm possible.

hints: Because the package can wait, arriving earlier at a node never hurts. That is the property Dijkstra's algorithm needs, with arrival minutes as distances.

For one lane, the best arrival when the package is ready at t is the smallest depart + transit over departures at or after t. That is not always the next departure. Sort the departures, keep suffix minima, and binary search for t.
With daily schedules, only today's remaining departures and tomorrow's departures can matter. Any later day offers the same departures, only later.
followups: Trucks have limited room, and packages compete for the last slots on a departure. Does your algorithm still give a correct promise, and what would you change?
Transit times vary from day to day. How would you promise a date that holds 95% of the time, and what data would you need?
This runs for millions of packages an hour from a few hundred origins. What would you precompute, and how would you keep it fresh when schedules change?
A linehaul is cancelled two hours before departure. How do you find the packages whose promise is now at risk, and what do you recompute?

rules.ask: The next departure leaves at minute 600 and arrives at 900. A later one leaves at 630 and arrives at 720. Which one does your code take, and why?
BFS finds the route with the fewest hops. Show a case where that route arrives later than another one.
How many passes does that take on a route of 3 000 hops, and how much work is each pass?
A transit takes 1 500 minutes and the package is ready at minute 1 430. Does your arithmetic still give the right day?
Dijkstra needs a property of the edge costs. State it for this problem, and say what would break it.

templates.title: Debug the fulfilment-centre inventory reservation processor
templates.subtopic: reservations, state checks, boundaries, keys

sections.scenario: When a customer places an order, the marketplace reserves units at a fulfilment centre so that the same unit is not promised twice. Shipping consumes the reservation, and cancelling releases it. The availability shown to customers is units on hand minus units reserved. Operations has raised several complaints about one processor. Some centres show units reserved for orders that shipped weeks ago. The last unit of popular items is never sold. A centre that is oversold after a damage write-off shows 0 available, not a negative number. Multi-item orders leave one line reserved after the customer cancels the other line. Availability creeps upward when customers press cancel twice. The processor below is the suspect.
sections.problem:
Fix process_inventory(events) so that it meets this specification. events is a list of dicts in commit order for one region. {{replay_rule}}

  1. receive {"type", "fc", "sku", "qty"} adds qty to on_hand at that centre for that SKU. adjust has the same shape, and its qty may be negative, for example damaged units. It changes on_hand only, never a reservation, so availability may become negative.
  2. reserve {"type", "order", "fc", "sku", "qty"} is one order line. It is accepted if and only if qty is at most the available units (on_hand − reserved) for that centre and SKU. If accepted, reserved increases by qty. If not, [order, sku] is appended to rejected. An order can have several lines, at most one per SKU, and a line is identified by (order, sku).
  3. cancel {"type", "order", "sku"} releases the line's reservation (reserved −= qty) only if the line is currently reserved, and the line becomes cancelled. A cancel for a line that is shipped, already cancelled, rejected or unknown changes nothing.
  4. ship {"type", "order", "sku"} applies only to a currently reserved line. It removes the units from stock: on_hand −= qty and reserved −= qty. The line becomes shipped.
  5. Output. {"stock": {"<fc>/<sku>": {"on_hand", "reserved", "available"}}, "rejected": [[order, sku], ...]}. stock has an entry for every centre and SKU named in a receive, adjust or reserve event. available is on_hand − reserved, reported as is, even when negative. rejected is in event order.
sections.constraints: Keep the function's shape and output format. Up to 200 000 events, processed in linear time.
sections.assumptions: Event types and quantities are hypothetical and simplified. Each event is delivered once and in order. Returns are a separate flow and do not appear here.
sections.criteria: Finds and explains every bug with its business symptom; a ship releases the reservation as well as stock; the last unit can be reserved; negative availability is reported, not clamped; lines keyed by (order, sku); a cancel releases only a reserved line; the fix stays minimal and linear; adds a test per bug.

clarifications.q: Can availability be negative?
clarifications.a: Yes, after a negative adjustment. Report it as is: a negative number tells operations the centre is oversold.

clarifications.q: Is an order line identified by its order id?
clarifications.a: By (order, sku). One order can reserve several SKUs.

clarifications.q: Can a rejected line be cancelled or shipped later?
clarifications.a: No. A cancel or ship for a rejected or unknown line is ignored.

clarifications.q: What does a cancel after shipping do?
clarifications.a: Nothing. Returns are handled elsewhere.

clarifications.q: How many bugs are there?
clarifications.a: Several, of different kinds. The checks point at each one.

hints: Write out on_hand, reserved and available after receive 5, reserve 2, ship. Then compare with what the code reports.
Read the availability check at its boundary: there are 3 units, and someone reserves 3.
What identifies a line? Make an order with two SKUs and cancel only one of them.
List the states a line can be in, and the states a cancel may move it out of.
followups: Two order services reserve the last unit at the same moment, in different processes. Where do you serialise, and what does a conditional UPDATE … WHERE on_hand - reserved >= :qty give you?
After a consumer restart, the event stream is redelivered from an earlier offset. Which events are already safe to apply twice, and what would you add for the others?
Reservations from abandoned checkouts never receive a cancel. How would you expire them, and what goes wrong if you expire them too early?
A centre shows negative availability after a damage write-off. Which orders should be moved to another centre first, who decides, and what does the customer see?

rules.ask: Your lock is inside one process. What happens when two hosts process events for the same SKU, and what key would you partition the stream by?
Who needs to see a negative availability number, and what decision would they make with it?
What happens if the same SKU appears on two lines of one order, and how would you change the key if that became allowed?
Is a ship event safe to apply twice with your fix? Is a receive? What would you store to make receives safe?

templates.title: Reconciling marketplace orders, payment settlements and refunds
templates.subtopic: batch matching, late data, re-issued reports, idempotent reruns

sections.scenario: A marketplace takes about {{daily_orders}} orders a day from first- and third-party sellers, in {{currencies}} currencies. A customer's payment is charged when items ship, so an order split into three shipments has three charges. Third-party sellers are paid their proceeds, sales minus marketplace fees, in settlements {{settlement_cycle}}, and each settlement comes with a report of the lines it covers. Refunds for returns can come up to {{refund_window}} after the sale, often in a later settlement period than the sale itself. Finance wants a daily answer for every order line: was it charged, was the seller settled, and was a refund handled correctly?
sections.problem: Design the pipeline that reconciles three sources every day: order and shipment events from the marketplace, charges and refunds from the payment processor, and settlement reports for {{sellers}} sellers. Cover how each source lands and is versioned, the keys you match on and at what grain, the states a line can be in (matched, timing difference, amount mismatch, missing on one side), partial shipments and partial refunds, currencies, re-issued reports, reruns and backfills that give the same answer for the same inputs, and the outputs finance and seller support use.
sections.constraints: Amounts are integer minor units in the transaction currency. A settlement report for a period can be re-issued with corrections. Payment files can arrive up to a day late and occasionally twice. Any past day must be re-runnable without double counting. Every unmatched line must carry a reason a person can act on.
sections.assumptions: All volumes, cycles, windows and fee structures are hypothetical. Each charge and refund from the payment processor carries the marketplace's own shipment or refund reference. Settlement reports list one row per order line, fee or adjustment with an amount and a type.
sections.criteria: Immutable, versioned landing of all three sources; a matching grain justified by how charges, settlements and refunds are actually produced; explicit states including timing differences with expected resolution; partial shipments and refunds handled per line; currency differences separated from breaks; deterministic, overwrite-by-partition reruns; versioned settlement reports with change explanations; outputs designed for both finance and seller support; a plan for each incident.

clarifications.q: Is the grain the order, the shipment or the line?
clarifications.a: Charges happen per shipment, settlement rows are per line and fee, and refunds are per returned line. You choose the matching grain, and you must explain it.

clarifications.q: How late can a refund be?
clarifications.a: Up to {{refund_window}} after the sale, and it can land in any later settlement period.

clarifications.q: What does a re-issued settlement report look like?
clarifications.a: The same seller and period with a new version number. Some rows change, some are added and some disappear.

clarifications.q: Do amounts ever differ legitimately?
clarifications.a: Yes. Currency conversion for settlement, rounding of fees per line versus per order, and partial refunds all cause differences you must explain, not hide.

clarifications.q: Who reads the output?
clarifications.a: Finance needs totals and ageing of breaks. Seller support needs to explain one seller's settlement line by line.

hints: Land every file as received, immutable and versioned, before you transform anything. A rerun should read exactly the versions it read the first time unless you ask for newer ones.
Match at the finest grain all three sources share, then roll up. A timing difference is a state with an expected resolution date, not a break.
Make each day's result a pure function of its inputs: rebuild a day's partition and overwrite it, never append to it.
followups: A settlement report for a closed period is re-issued with corrected fees. What does your pipeline recompute, and what does finance see about the change?
An order line was shipped in two shipments and refunded in part twice. Walk through the rows each source produces and how they match.
Settlement happens in a different currency from the sale. Where does conversion happen, which rate do you use, and how do you separate a conversion difference from a real break?
Finance asks for the first day's results to be reproduced exactly, six months later, for an audit. What must you have kept?
Matching at {{daily_orders}} orders a day takes longer every week because unmatched lines accumulate. How do you bound the work?

rules.ask: An order has three shipments, one cancelled line and one partial refund. What does a join at the order level hide?
Day 12 is rerun after a late payment file. How does your table avoid counting day 12's matches twice?
Which amounts in your pipeline are stored as what type, and where could a fraction of a minor unit appear?
Which day's rate do you use for a refund that is 60 days after the sale, and does the seller's settlement agree?
A re-issued report replaces the old one. How do you still explain to a seller why last month's statement changed?

incidents: Settlements run {{settlement_cycle}}. One period's report for one currency is re-issued three days after it was matched, with corrected fee rows, and finance has already closed that period.
The payment processor's refund file for one day arrives twice; the second copy has 2% more rows because late refunds were added.
A deploy changes the format of shipment references. For one day, charges stop matching shipments and the break count jumps by two orders of magnitude.

templates.title: Centralised log pipeline for many cloud accounts
templates.subtopic: multi-tenant ingestion, partitioning, compaction, retention

query_target: in under 10 seconds for the last hour
in under a minute for the last day

sections.scenario: Public cloud platforms offer managed log services: agents on customers' servers and functions send application and access logs, and customers search them and keep them for a chosen retention period. You are designing the ingestion and storage pipeline for such a service in one region. It serves {{accounts}} customer accounts sending about {{ingest}} of raw log lines. Each account sets a retention period, by default {{retention}}. Customers expect to find a request id {{query_target}}.
sections.problem: Design the pipeline from the agent's batch upload to queryable storage. Cover the ingestion API and what makes a batch retry harmless, the durable buffer and how it is partitioned, parsing and enrichment, storage layout (a recent hot tier and compressed columnar files in object storage), how files are partitioned and compacted, late and out-of-order timestamps, isolation between tenants, retention deletion per account, and the metrics that tell you the pipeline is healthy.
sections.constraints: One account must never see another's logs. A noisy account must not delay others. Agents retry, so the same batch can arrive more than once. Log timestamps can be hours late, or in the future because of clock skew on a host. Expired data must be deleted within a day of expiry. Cost per stored and scanned gigabyte matters as much as latency.
sections.assumptions: All volumes, account counts and targets are hypothetical. Each agent batch carries the account, a log group, a stream name, a batch sequence number and up to a few thousand lines with timestamps. You may use common open building blocks (a partitioned log, a stream processor, object storage, a columnar format, an inverted index or a scan engine).
sections.criteria: Batch identity and a bounded deduplication store that makes retries harmless; a buffer partitioned for isolation with per-account quotas; partitions keyed so queries and per-account retention deletes are cheap; a compaction plan with atomic file swaps; late data written by event time with a clear rule for very late or future timestamps; tenant isolation enforced at write and read; exact per-account byte accounting; useful health metrics (lag, rejects, small-file count, deletion backlog); a plan for each incident.

clarifications.q: Do customers query by time only, or by content too?
clarifications.a: Both: a time range plus filters on fields or free text, and finding one request id is the most common query.

clarifications.q: Which timestamp counts, the line's or the arrival time?
clarifications.a: Customers search by the line's timestamp. You also record arrival time.

clarifications.q: Must the order of lines within a stream be preserved?
clarifications.a: Within one stream, yes, by the line's timestamp and then the order in the batch.

clarifications.q: Can a customer change retention?
clarifications.a: Yes, at any time, longer or shorter. A shorter period applies to data already stored.

clarifications.q: Is per-account cost reported?
clarifications.a: Yes. Ingested and stored bytes per account and log group are billed, so they must be exact.

hints: Make the agent's (account, log group, stream, sequence number) the identity of a batch, and decide where you remember which ones you have seen.
Partition storage so that both common queries and retention deletes touch as few files as possible: think about what the first partition key should be.
Small files are the main cost and latency risk of a streaming writer. Plan when and how they are merged, and what readers see during the merge.
followups: One account starts sending ten times its usual volume. Walk through what each stage does, and what every other account notices.
Lines arrive two days late. Where are they written, how do customers find them, and what does that do to your compaction?
A customer shortens retention from {{retention}} to 7 days. What do you delete, how fast, and how do you prove it is gone?
How do you make ingested-bytes billing exact when batches are retried and some lines are dropped as malformed?
Search for a request id over a whole day is slow for the largest accounts. What index or layout change would you make, and what does it cost to maintain?

rules.ask: A retention delete for one account must not rewrite other accounts' data. With your layout, what does deleting one account's expired day cost?
What is your partition key, and what happens to the other tenants on that partition when one account's volume jumps?
How long do you remember batch identities, and what happens to a retried batch that arrives after that window?
A compaction job rewrites files that a customer's query is reading. What does the query see, and how is that made safe?
What does indexing every field cost at {{ingest}}, and which fields would you index instead?

incidents: One account's debug logging is switched on by mistake, and within ten minutes it sends 40% of the region's {{ingest}}.
After a network partition, agents on thousands of hosts retry, and twenty minutes of batches arrive twice.
A customer reports that lines with timestamps two days in the past are missing from searches of that day.

templates.title: Orders that split, ship and come back line by line
templates.subtopic: order-line grain, partial cancellations and returns, OLTP to facts

sections.scenario: A marketplace sells items from its own retail business (first party) and from independent sellers (third party, about {{third_party_share}} of units here). Customers place about {{daily_orders}} orders a day. An order holds several line items; a line can be fulfilled by the marketplace's network or by the seller, and about {{split_share}} of orders split into more than one shipment. Before a line ships, the customer can cancel the whole order or part of a line's quantity; after delivery they can return some or all units within {{return_window_days}} days, and in this scenario a refund can be issued as soon as a return is started, before the item is received back. Seller, category and finance teams all report on these orders, and each has its own idea of "net units sold".
sections.problem: Design the data model from the transactional system to the analytical facts. Cover: the OLTP entities (order, order line, shipment and its lines, cancellation, return and its lines, refund) with their keys and the quantity invariants that hold between them; how changes are captured so that history is not lost; the fact tables and their grains that answer "net ordered units and net sales by day, seller and category", "cancellation rate before shipment", "return rate by seller and category" and "refunds issued for items not yet received back"; and one written definition of net units sold that all three teams can use.
sections.constraints: Quantities on a line reconcile: ordered = cancelled + shipped + still open, and returned ≤ shipped. The refunded amount for a line never exceeds what was charged for it. Money is stored as integers in minor units. A line's state at any past time must be reconstructable. Seller-facing numbers for a closed month change only by a documented restatement.
sections.assumptions: Volumes, shares and the return window are hypothetical. Prices, promotions and taxes are carried per line; an order-level promotion is allocated to its lines when the order is placed. A first-party line carries the retail business as its seller, so every line has exactly one seller.
sections.criteria: Order line as the grain with explicit quantity invariants; quantity movements kept as rows or events so history survives; shipments, returns and refunds as separate entities referencing the line; refunds decoupled from receipt of the return; facts at stated grains (movement fact and/or accumulating snapshot per line) with conformed seller, category and date dimensions; one precise net-units definition; a cohort, denominator and close for return rates; seller-level access; each incident contained, corrected and guarded.

clarifications.q: Can one line ship in more than one shipment?
clarifications.a: Yes. A line of 3 units can ship 2 now and 1 later, possibly from different fulfilment centres.

clarifications.q: What does a return reference?
clarifications.a: The order line, and the shipment when it is known. A replacement for a damaged unit is a new shipment against the same line with no new charge.

clarifications.q: Which date does a return count on?
clarifications.a: Your choice. Say whether rates are reported by the date the units shipped (a cohort) or the date of the return (activity), and why.

clarifications.q: Can a line be cancelled after it ships?
clarifications.a: No. After shipment the customer returns it or refuses the delivery, and a refused delivery comes back as a return.

clarifications.q: Do sellers see each other's numbers?
clarifications.a: No. A seller sees only their own lines, never the first-party ones.

hints: Choose the grain first: the order line is the unit of truth for quantity and money; the order is a header.
Record quantity movements on a line (cancelled, shipped, returned, refunded) as their own rows instead of overwriting counters on the line.
A return rate needs a cohort and a denominator: returns of units shipped in a period, or returns received in a period, answer different questions.
followups: Write the invariant ordered = cancelled + shipped + open as a check. Where does it run, and what happens to a line that breaks it?
A replacement ships for a damaged unit and the customer then returns the replacement. How many units were shipped and returned, and what does the return rate show?
An order-level promotion was allocated across three lines. The line that qualified the order for it is cancelled. What happens to the other lines' allocated amounts and to net sales already reported?
Returns arrive up to {{return_window_days}} days after delivery. When is a month's return rate final, and what do you show before then?
At {{daily_orders}} orders a day, would you keep an accumulating snapshot per line, append-only movement facts, or both? How do you keep the warehouse cheap to update?

rules.ask: One order has a line that shipped, a line that was half cancelled and a line that was returned. What does your row per order say about each, and how does a seller see only their own line?
A line of 3 units had 1 cancelled, 2 shipped and 1 returned. If the status is overwritten, how do you answer "how many units were open last Tuesday"?
Is your denominator units shipped, units ordered or orders? Which cohort, and what happens to the most recent month?
The refund was issued when the return started, but the item never came back. Where does that show in your model, and who sees it?
The OLTP system updates the same line row several times within a second. What do you capture, and how do you avoid losing an intermediate state?

incidents: A seller's dashboard shows a return rate above 100% for one category: replacement shipments were matched as returns of the original line but never counted as shipments.
After promotion amounts were re-allocated on partial cancellations, last month's net sales by seller no longer sum to the finance total. The month was already closed and statements went to sellers.
With {{split_share}} of orders splitting into several shipments, an upstream release starts re-numbering shipment lines on every update, and the warehouse counts split lines twice.

templates.title: Seller inbound shipments — declared, received and reconciled units
templates.subtopic: declared versus observed quantities, receiving events, discrepancy cases

sections.scenario: Third-party sellers who use the marketplace's fulfilment service send their stock to its fulfilment centres. A seller creates an inbound shipment plan listing SKUs and quantities; the plan can be split across several fulfilment centres; the seller then ships labelled boxes, each with declared contents. A fulfilment centre receives a shipment over several days (here receiving normally finishes within {{receive_days}} days of the first box arriving), scanning units as they are checked in and put away, and finds some units missing, extra, damaged or unlabelled. About {{daily_inbound_units}} units arrive a day from {{sellers}} active sellers, and about {{discrepancy_share}} of units end up in a discrepancy. Sellers want to see, per shipment and SKU, what they sent, what was received and what is still being investigated; the marketplace must resolve every shortfall, either by finding the units, reimbursing the seller, or recording that the seller's declaration was wrong.
sections.problem: Design the data model: shipment plans and their versions (a seller can edit quantities until the shipment is marked shipped), the split into one shipment per fulfilment centre, boxes and their declared contents, receiving events (box arrivals, unit check-ins, damage found), and discrepancy cases with their lifecycle (opened, investigating, found, reimbursed, closed as a declaration error). Define the reconciliation invariant per shipment and SKU, when a shipment is closed, and the facts that answer "units in transit versus received, per seller", "time from first box arrival to units sellable", "discrepancy rate by seller, carrier and fulfilment centre" and "units and amounts reimbursed".
sections.constraints: For every shipment and SKU, declared units are eventually fully accounted for: received sellable + received damaged + found later + reimbursed + declaration error, with nothing left open after the investigation window. Receiving history is immutable. A seller sees only their own shipments. Reimbursements are money in integer minor units. Receiving events can arrive late and more than once.
sections.assumptions: Volumes, seller counts, windows and shares are hypothetical. Each unit carries a label that identifies the seller's SKU, so stock from different sellers is never pooled in this scenario. A box can contain several SKUs. A unit received under the wrong shipment can be matched to the right one later.
sections.criteria: Declared, observed and resolved quantities kept apart; plans versioned with the shipped version frozen; per-fulfilment-centre shipments and boxes with declared contents; append-only receiving events deduplicated by id; discrepancy cases with typed resolutions and an invariant per shipment and SKU; "received" and "sellable" defined; facts at stated grains with a cohort and a close for rates; seller-level access; each incident contained, corrected and guarded.

clarifications.q: Can a seller change the plan after shipping?
clarifications.a: No. Quantities can be edited until the shipment is marked shipped; afterwards only a box-contents correction with evidence is accepted.

clarifications.q: What happens to a unit that no plan mentions?
clarifications.a: It is received as an unexpected unit, held, and matched to a shipment later when possible.

clarifications.q: When is a missing unit declared lost?
clarifications.a: After an investigation window (your choice, stated); then it is reimbursed or closed as a declaration error.

clarifications.q: Are boxes always delivered where they were planned?
clarifications.a: No. A box can arrive at the wrong fulfilment centre, or with contents that differ from the declaration.

clarifications.q: Does "received" mean scanned at the dock or available for sale?
clarifications.a: Define both. Sellers care most about when units become sellable.

hints: Separate what was declared (plan and box contents, versioned) from what was observed (receiving events) and from how gaps were resolved (discrepancy cases). The reconciled view is derived from the three.
The invariant lives at shipment × SKU; each discrepancy case closes part of the gap with a typed resolution.
Receiving events are append-only with an event id, so late and repeated scans are harmless.
followups: Write the reconciliation invariant and show the derived view for one SKU: 100 declared, 96 checked in sellable, 2 damaged, and 1 found a week later under another shipment.
A seller edited the plan twice before shipping. Which version do you reconcile against, and how do you show the edits?
A plan was split across three fulfilment centres and one receives a box meant for another. How does your model match it?
Define the discrepancy rate precisely, including the cohort and when a shipment's number is final given receiving that takes up to {{receive_days}} days.
At {{daily_inbound_units}} units a day, unit check-in events dominate storage. Which grain does the warehouse keep for years, and what is aggregated?

rules.ask: Two scanners check in the same box at once and one scan is redelivered an hour later. How does your counter stay right, and how do you show the seller the history?
The plan is split across three fulfilment centres and one box arrives at the wrong one. Where does that box live in your model?
A reimbursed unit is found two weeks later. What happens to the reimbursement and to the seller's inventory?
Is the denominator declared units or received units, and which shipments are still too young to count?
What exactly is versioned: the plan, the box contents or the receiving counts? Which of these may never change after the fact?

incidents: A carrier delivers a region's pallets to the wrong fulfilment centre. For {{receive_days}} days the planned shipments show missing units, and automated discrepancy cases open for thousands of sellers.
A scanner firmware update redelivers a day of unit check-ins. Received exceeds declared for about {{discrepancy_share}} of shipments, and those sellers' sellable inventory jumps.
Reimbursements were paid for units that were later found and put away. The seller's inventory counts them as sellable while the reimbursement stays paid.

templates.title: Forecasts as data — issued runs, quantiles and accuracy against censored demand
templates.subtopic: forecast runs and values, immutability, accuracy metrics, censored actuals

sections.scenario: A retailer issues a weekly demand forecast for {{series}} item-and-region series, {{horizon_weeks}} weeks ahead, as probabilistic quantiles ({{quantiles}}). Buying and stock-placement decisions read the issued forecast. Several model versions run side by side: the production model and challengers. Actual sales arrive daily and are corrected later for returns and late orders. In about {{stockout_share}} of series-weeks the item was out of stock for part of the week, so sales understate demand. Planners want to know which forecast drove a decision; the forecasting team wants accuracy by horizon, category and model version.
sections.problem: Design the data model for forecasts and their evaluation. Cover: how a forecast run is stored (model version, forecast date, the feature snapshot it read, status) and how its values are stored (grain, keys, immutability); how challenger runs and re-runs are kept apart from what was issued; planner overrides; the actuals, with their corrections and the in-stock share of each week; and the accuracy layer: which metrics (for example a volume-weighted absolute percentage error for the median, bias, and quantile loss or coverage for the other quantiles), at which grain, against which version of actuals, and how censored weeks are treated. Estimate the storage at series × horizon × quantile × forecast date and say what you keep at full grain.
sections.constraints: An issued forecast is never overwritten: a planner can always see exactly what was issued on a date. Accuracy is reproducible: re-running an evaluation gives the same number unless the actuals it reads were restated, and the report says which actuals it used. Exactly one run per forecast date is the issued production forecast.
sections.assumptions: Series counts, horizons, quantile sets and shares are hypothetical. Weeks are calendar weeks in the region's time zone. Model versions are immutable once registered. Availability data gives, for each series and week, the share of hours the item could be bought.
sections.criteria: Runs separated from values, with issued runs immutable and a unique issued run per forecast date; values in long form with horizon and quantile as keys; overrides as their own records; actuals versioned with availability; accuracy metrics defined with weighting, censoring treatment and the actuals version recorded; a storage estimate with partitioning and retention; each incident traced, corrected and guarded.

clarifications.q: Is a re-run of the same model on the same date a new forecast?
clarifications.a: It is a new run. Only one run per forecast date is marked issued, and only issued runs drive decisions.

clarifications.q: Which actuals does accuracy use, first reported or corrected?
clarifications.a: You decide. State when actuals are final and whether accuracy is restated afterwards.

clarifications.q: How do we know a week was censored?
clarifications.a: From the in-stock share of the week in the availability data.

clarifications.q: Do planners change forecasts?
clarifications.a: Sometimes, for a promotion they know about. An override is its own record with author and reason; the model's forecast is never edited.

clarifications.q: Which metric matters most?
clarifications.a: A volume-weighted error on the median for buying, and coverage or quantile loss for the quantiles that set safety stock. You choose the weighting.

hints: Separate runs (model version, forecast date, inputs snapshot, status) from values (run, series, target week, quantile, value). "Issued" is a status of a run, set once.
Store target week and horizon explicitly as rows, not columns per horizon or per quantile; most accuracy questions slice by horizon.
Accuracy joins values to actuals by series and target week. Decide whether censored weeks are excluded, down-weighted or compared with estimated demand, and record the choice with the result.
followups: Estimate rows per weekly issue at {{series}} series × {{horizon_weeks}} weeks × your quantiles. How do you partition and compress them, and what stays at full grain for how long?
A planner overrides the forecast for a promotion. How does accuracy treat the override versus the model, and who sees which number?
Returns arrive weeks later and lower last month's actuals. Which accuracy numbers change, and how is a report labelled?
A challenger beats production on the median error but its P90 covers actuals only 70% of the time. What does your model let the team see, and which decision does that inform?
In {{stockout_share}} of series-weeks the item was partly unavailable. Show how you avoid rewarding a forecast that predicted capped sales rather than demand.

rules.ask: A buyer asks what the forecast said on the day they placed a purchase order last month. With the latest forecast winning, can you answer?
A series sold 0 units in a week. What does MAPE do there, and how does your metric handle low-volume series?
Do you drop censored weeks, down-weight them or estimate demand? What bias does each choice put into the accuracy report?
The team adds a P98 quantile and extends the horizon. What happens to your table and to the rows already written?
Which version of actuals does a reproducible accuracy run read, and where is that recorded?

incidents: A debugging re-run of last week's production model was marked issued by mistake. Purchase orders covering the next {{horizon_weeks}} weeks of one category now trace to a forecast nobody reviewed, and the original issued run cannot be told apart from it.

Reported accuracy for the latest month improved sharply during a stockout wave: in {{stockout_share}} of series-weeks sales were capped by availability, so forecasts that under-predicted demand looked accurate.
A returns backfill restated two months of actuals. Last quarter's model comparison, already used to promote a challenger, now favours the previous production model.

templates.title: Seller settlements — orders, fees, refunds and disbursements that reconcile
templates.subtopic: settlement periods, typed transaction lines, reserves, three-way reconciliation

reserve_rule: a reserve of 5% of each period's sales, released 30 days later
a reserve equal to the refunds expected over the next 7 days

sections.scenario: A marketplace collects payment from customers on behalf of third-party sellers and pays sellers on a settlement cycle, here every {{settlement_days}} days. Each period a seller receives a statement of transactions: order principal, shipping and tax collected, marketplace fees (a commission on each sale, and fulfilment fees where the marketplace ships the order), refunds with their fee adjustments, reimbursements for lost or damaged inventory, promotion costs and other charges such as storage. In this scenario the marketplace holds back {{reserve_rule}}. The net amount is disbursed to the seller's bank account; a disbursement can fail and be retried. There are about {{monthly_transactions}} transactions a month across {{sellers}} sellers.
sections.problem: Design the data model that lets the marketplace's finance team and each seller reconcile three things: the operational events (orders shipped, refunds issued), the settlement transaction lines (what was posted, to which period), and the disbursements (bank transfers and their outcomes). Cover the settlement period and its lifecycle (open, closed, disbursement sent, paid, failed, retried), transaction lines with types and signs, the reserve as its own balance, the keys that link each line to its order or refund and to its period, a reconciliation status per order, and the timing differences (an order shipped on the last day of a period settles in the next).
sections.constraints: A closed period's statement never changes; corrections appear as new lines in a later period. For each period, opening balance + Σ lines − change in reserve − amount disbursed = closing balance, carried forward when negative. Money is stored as integers in minor units, per currency; a seller can sell in several marketplaces with different currencies, and amounts in different currencies are never added. Every line is traceable to its source event.
sections.assumptions: Seller counts, cycles, volumes and the reserve rule are hypothetical; the fee schedule itself is out of scope. In this scenario an order's money posts when it ships, not when it is placed.
sections.criteria: Periods and typed signed lines with balances derived, never edited; the balance equation per period and currency; the reserve as its own balance with an auditable rule; keys from every line to its source event and period; reconciliation status per order through posting and payment; event, posting and period times kept apart; disbursement lifecycle with failures returning funds; each incident contained and corrected with compensating lines, not edits.

clarifications.q: When does an order's money post?
clarifications.a: At shipment in this scenario. An order cancelled before shipment never posts.

clarifications.q: Can a period's net be negative?
clarifications.a: Yes, after heavy refunds. The negative balance carries forward to the next period in this scenario.

clarifications.q: Does a refund return the marketplace fee?
clarifications.a: Partly. In this scenario most of the commission is returned and a small administration fee is kept, so model fee lines separately from principal.

clarifications.q: What happens when a disbursement fails?
clarifications.a: The amount returns to the seller's balance and is paid by a retry or in the next period.

clarifications.q: Which time zone defines a period?
clarifications.a: You decide; the seller's reports are in their marketplace's local time.

hints: Treat each seller's statement as a small ledger: periods, typed signed lines, and balances (available and reserved) derived from lines.
Reconciliation is a status per source item: an order is posted when its lines appear in a period, and paid when that period's disbursement succeeds.
Keep event time, posting time and period apart. Most reconciliation breaks are timing.
followups: Write the period balance equation and walk one period that contains a refund for an order sold in the previous period and a failed disbursement.
An order ships at 23:59 local time on the last day of a period whose boundary is defined in UTC. Which period gets it, and how does the seller see why?
A refund is issued for an order whose sale posted three periods ago. Which lines are created, with which keys, and how does the seller see the net result of that order?
Finance must prove every day that order postings equal operational shipments, by marketplace and currency. Which tables and keys make that one query?
The reserve rule changes in the middle of a period. How is the change auditable, and how does the seller see why the payout dropped?

rules.ask: A refund and a sale post for the same seller at the same moment. How does the balance stay right, and how does it appear on a statement that must never change?
A posted fee was wrong. How do you correct it without changing the closed statement the seller already downloaded?
Two orders for the same amount on the same day: how do you avoid matching the wrong one, and which key would remove the guess?
The seller's dashboard counts local days and your periods use another boundary. How do you keep their totals from disagreeing?
Is the reserve a separate balance or just a line type? How does its release show up on a later statement?

incidents: A bank rejects a batch of disbursements because of a changed account format, but the {{settlement_days}}-day periods were marked paid when the transfers were sent. Sellers see "paid" for money they did not receive.
A fee change was applied twice in one period for 3% of sellers. Their statements are closed and already downloaded.
For orders that shipped at a period boundary, refund lines arrived before the sale lines, and per-order reconciliation shows thousands of "refund without sale" breaks.

templates.title: Available to promise from an inventory ledger and reservation holds
templates.subtopic: ledger sums, reservation holds, as-of boundaries, at-least-once feeds

sections.scenario: A marketplace keeps sellable stock in fulfilment centres (here {{fc_list}}). Every physical change is a row in the inventory movement ledger with a signed qty: positive puts units on the shelf, negative takes them off. {{kinds_rule}} When an order is assigned to a fulfilment centre, a reservation holds units of the SKU there until they ship. A hold lapses at expires_at ({{ttl_hours}} hours after it was made) and a cancelled order releases it. Operations wants a point-in-time view of what each fulfilment centre can still promise, and of where more units are held than are on the shelf.
sections.problem: Write one PostgreSQL query that returns fc_id, sku, on_hand, reserved, available_to_promise, oversold_units as of {{as_of}}: one row per (fc_id, sku) that has a movement that occurred at or before that time, or a reservation made at or before it, ordered by fc_id, sku. on_hand is the sum of qty over the pair's movements with occurred_at at or before the as-of time. reserved is the sum, over the pair's reservations made at or before the as-of time, of the units each still holds: its qty minus the units shipped against it (ship movements carrying its reservation_id that occurred at or before the as-of time), never below 0. A reservation holds nothing if it was cancelled at or before the as-of time, or if it has expired: it holds only while the as-of time is strictly before expires_at. available_to_promise is on_hand − reserved and oversold_units is reserved − on_hand, each floored at 0. {{feed_rule}}
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). Boundaries are inclusive, except expiry: at exactly expires_at the hold has lapsed. A pair whose reserved units are all released still appears. The sample has {{movements}} movement rows and {{reservations}} reservations; production has billions of movements across hundreds of fulfilment centres.
sections.assumptions: Hypothetical schema, fulfilment centres, SKUs and quantities. A ship movement's fc_id and sku always match its reservation's. Quantities are units; no money is involved.
sections.criteria: Movements and holds aggregated separately and combined with a FULL JOIN; units shipped subtracted from each hold, floored at 0; cancellation and expiry boundaries exactly as stated; floored outputs; at the hardest level, one row per event_id and occurred_at (not ingested_at) as the time; deterministic ordering; can explain materialised balances, the sweeper gap and how to allocate an oversell to orders.

clarifications.q: Does a reservation made exactly at the as-of time hold units?
clarifications.a: Yes. Made at or before the as-of time counts.

clarifications.q: And one cancelled exactly at the as-of time?
clarifications.a: It is released: cancelled at or before the as-of time holds nothing.

clarifications.q: Should I filter on ingested_at?
clarifications.a: No. occurred_at places an event in time; ingested_at is only when it reached the warehouse.

clarifications.q: Should a pair with reservations but no movements yet appear?
clarifications.a: Yes, with on_hand 0. Those are the rows operations cares about most.

clarifications.q: Does shipping a reserved unit change both on_hand and reserved?
clarifications.a: Yes. The ship movement takes it off the shelf and consumes that much of the hold, so the unit is never subtracted twice.

hints: First compute the units shipped per reservation from ship movements up to the as-of time, then each reservation's remaining hold.
Aggregate movements and holds separately by (fc_id, sku) and combine the two with a FULL JOIN. Joining raw movements to raw reservations multiplies rows.
GREATEST(x, 0) floors a value; COALESCE fills the side that is missing.
followups: At billions of movements, how would you serve this per (fulfilment centre, SKU) in milliseconds, and what keeps a materialised balance exactly equal to the ledger?
This query treats a hold as released the instant it expires; the operational system releases it when a sweeper runs. Which number is right for the storefront, and which for this report?
A SKU shows oversold units. Write the follow-on query that lists which reservations, oldest first, cannot be filled from on_hand.
The feed is at least once. Should duplicates be removed in this query, at ingestion, or both? What does each cost?

rules.ask: How many rows does one reservation produce when it is joined to every movement of its SKU, and what does that do to your SUM?
Which (fc_id, sku) rows disappear with an inner join, and are they the ones operations needs most?
What exactly is DISTINCT removing? Two genuine receipts of the same quantity can differ only in event_id.
Why can ingested_at be later than occurred_at, and which of the two belongs in an as-of filter for physical stock?
At exactly expires_at, is the hold still in force? Show the comparison you wrote and why.

incidents: During a deal, this report shows oversold units for one SKU at one fulfilment centre while the storefront kept promising delivery; the storefront's cached availability lagged the reservations by minutes, and holds last {{ttl_hours}} hours.

After a consumer restart the movement feed redelivered an hour of ship events. A version of this report that summed raw rows showed on_hand below zero for a few SKUs and triggered re-planning of orders that could have shipped.

templates.title: Inventory availability and reservations during a lightning deal
templates.subtopic: inventory reservations, hot keys, reconciliation

sections.scenario: A marketplace ships items from {{fcs}} fulfilment centres, alongside third-party sellers who hold their own stock. Stock in a fulfilment centre changes all day: receiving, picks, damages, transfers between centres, customer returns put back on the shelf, and adjustments when a cycle count finds the shelf disagrees with the system. Product pages show whether an item is in stock and when it can arrive; checkout must not accept an order that no fulfilment centre can fill. A lightning deal offers {{deal_units}} units of one item at a discount for a short window. Marketplace-wide orders peak at {{peak_orders}} per second, and in the first minute of the deal a large share of them are for that one item.
sections.problem: Design the inventory availability system.
