Cover the source of truth for on-hand stock per item and fulfilment centre; the available-to-promise number (on hand, minus reserved, minus anything held back); reservations taken when an order is placed and released when it is cancelled, when payment fails, or when it is not confirmed within {{hold_minutes}} minutes; the read path for product pages; the write path for checkout; and reconciliation with physical counts. Say how a single deal item with thousands of orders per second is handled without overselling.
sections.constraints: The deal must never sell more than {{deal_units}} units. Product page availability reads p99 under 20 ms and may be a few seconds stale; the checkout reservation decision p99 under 200 ms and must be exact. A fulfilment centre can lose connectivity to the central systems for several minutes and keeps picking, receiving and counting while disconnected. Every unit change must be traceable to the event that caused it.
sections.assumptions: All volumes, timings and counts are hypothetical. Each fulfilment centre runs a warehouse system that is the authority for what is physically on its shelves and emits stock-change events. Payment authorisation is a separate service that answers in under a second, or times out.
sections.criteria: Separates the exact reservation path from the cached availability read path; stock as an append-only, idempotent change log with projections; atomic conditional decrements and a hot-key strategy (allotments with rebalancing, or a single-writer per deal) that cannot oversell; reservations with explicit states and expiry; idempotent retries keyed by order line; merge rules for disconnected centres and authority boundaries; reconciliation against physical counts with automatic re-sourcing; an audit that proves units sold; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: Is a reservation tied to a specific fulfilment centre?
clarifications.a: At order placement it can be tied to a region or a centre; you decide, and say what that costs you when a centre runs short.

clarifications.q: Do carts reserve stock?
clarifications.a: No. Only placed orders reserve.

clarifications.q: Can the product page show "in stock" when the last units are reserved but unpaid?
clarifications.a: Your call; say what customers see and why.

clarifications.q: What happens to an order whose reserved unit turns out not to exist?
clarifications.a: It is re-sourced from another centre if possible; otherwise it is delayed or cancelled with notice. Both cost money and trust.

clarifications.q: Do third-party sellers' own stock counts go through the same system?
clarifications.a: Their counts arrive as feeds and API updates; treat them as less timely and less trusted than a fulfilment centre's.

hints: Separate the exact, low-volume write path (reservations) from the approximate, very high-volume read path (product pages). They need different stores and different guarantees.
One row decremented thousands of times a second is a hot key. Think about splitting a deal's units into several independently decremented allotments.
Model stock as an append-only log of changes keyed by event id; the counts are a projection of it. That gives you idempotency, replay and an audit trail.
followups: Walk through one checkout for the deal item: which records change, in what order, and what makes the decrement exact when two requests race for the last unit?
Splitting the deal's units into allotments helps throughput, but one allotment can run dry while others still hold units. How do you rebalance without overselling?
A fulfilment centre reconnects after 25 minutes offline and sends its backlog. How do you merge it without double counting or losing a pick?
A cycle count shows a popular item is short at one centre, and some of the missing units are already promised to customers. What does the system do automatically?
How would you prove, after the event, that the deal sold exactly what it was allowed to and no more?

rules.ask: Thousands of checkouts per second wait on that one lock for the deal item. What is the p99 reservation latency now, and what do you change?
The cache node holding the deal counter fails mid-deal. What is the count on the replacement, and how do you know it has not oversold?
Which number in your design is allowed to be eventually consistent, and which one must never be? Show me where the boundary is.
The deal item lives on one partition and takes a large share of all writes in the first minute. What happens to the other items on that partition?
The process that releases expired reservations stalls for an hour. What do customers see, and what do you lose?

incidents: The deal opens and reservation latency for the deal item climbs to 4 seconds. Checkout clients time out and retry, and the reservation count for the item rises faster than orders are placed.
A cycle count at one fulfilment centre finds 1,200 fewer units of a best-selling item than the system shows; about 300 of them are already reserved for orders promised for tomorrow.
One of the {{fcs}} fulfilment centres is cut off from the central systems for 25 minutes during the deal and keeps picking and receiving.

The release of reservations not confirmed within {{hold_minutes}} minutes stops for an hour. The deal item shows sold out while more than a quarter of its {{deal_units}} units are held by expired reservations and sit unsold on shelves.

templates.title: Package tracking and delivery-promise accuracy platform
templates.subtopic: out-of-order scans, state machines, metric definition

sections.scenario: A retailer ships about {{packages}} packages a day through its own network and {{carriers}} external carriers. Each package collects about {{scans}} scan events on its way: packed and shipped at the fulfilment centre, sorted, loaded for line haul, received at a delivery station, out for delivery, and delivered or attempted, scanned by drivers' handheld devices. External carriers report through their own tracking feeds with their own status codes. Every order carries a promised delivery date set at checkout. Customers watch tracking pages; operations teams need a list of packages at risk of missing their promise within {{freshness}} of the scan that put them at risk; leadership reviews a daily promise-accuracy metric by region, carrier and shipping option.
sections.problem: Design the platform: ingestion from scanners and carrier feeds, normalisation into one status model, the current state and full history of each package, the customer tracking read path, at-risk detection, and the daily promise-accuracy metric. Define the metric precisely and say how late or corrected events change it.
sections.constraints: Handheld devices buffer scans while offline, sometimes for hours, and send them later; events arrive out of order and some arrive twice. A delivered package can later be corrected (delivered to the wrong address, then recovered). Promise accuracy is measured by the end of the promised day in the delivery address's local time zone. Tracking pages p99 under 100 ms. The scan history of a package is kept for two years.
sections.assumptions: All volumes, counts and service levels are hypothetical. Every scan carries a package id, a scan code, a location, a device or carrier id, a device timestamp, and the time the platform received it.
sections.criteria: Normalised status model with an owned carrier-code mapping; per-package ordering by event time with duplicate handling; current state derived from history so late events cannot regress it; a precise, local-time promise-accuracy definition with a stated restatement policy; at-risk detection based on remaining legs, with alert budgets; tracking reads from a keyed store; device-time sanity checks; carrier feed health monitoring; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: Which timestamp counts, the device's or the platform's?
clarifications.a: You decide; device clocks are usually right but not always.

clarifications.q: What exactly is "on time"?
clarifications.a: Delivered on or before the promised date in the destination's local time. Attempts do not count as deliveries.

clarifications.q: Can a promised date change after checkout?
clarifications.a: Yes, when the customer is told of a delay. Leadership wants accuracy against the original promise, and operations also wants it against the latest one.

clarifications.q: How are carriers' status codes mapped?
clarifications.a: Each carrier publishes its codes; someone has to own a mapping, and new codes appear without warning.

clarifications.q: Is the metric allowed to change after the day is reported?
clarifications.a: That is a choice you must make and explain.

hints: A package is a state machine, but the current state must be derived from the history ordered by event time, not by arrival order.
Write down how each status (delivered, attempted, returned, lost) affects the metric before you design the pipeline that computes it.
"At risk" is a prediction: compare where the package is with where it needs to be to make the promise, given the remaining legs.
followups: A "delivered" scan arrives before the "out for delivery" scan for the same package. What does the tracking page show, and what is stored?
How do you compute the daily promise-accuracy metric so it is stable enough for leadership but still correct when scans arrive a day late?
How does at-risk detection work, and how do you keep it from flooding operations with alerts for packages that will still make it?
A carrier adds a new status code that your mapping does not know. What happens to those packages on the tracking page and in the metric?
Leadership asks why accuracy in one region dropped two points last week. What does the platform let you show them within an hour?

rules.ask: What do you key the stream by, and how does that key keep every scan for one package in order for the state machine?
An offline device uploads a scan from four hours ago after newer scans arrived. Does your latest-status update go backwards?
A package for an address eight hours west of UTC is delivered at 22:00 local time on the promised day. Is it on time in your metric?
Two scans have the same package, code and location, eleven seconds apart. Are they duplicates? What is your key?
How many at-risk alerts does your rule raise on a normal day, and who acts on each one?

incidents: A handheld app release stamps scans with the device clock, and devices in one region have clocks a day ahead. For 3% of that region's packages, "delivered" is recorded a day after the promise and the region's accuracy drops overnight.
One of the {{carriers}} external carriers' feeds stops for 9 hours, then sends the backlog at once. During the gap the at-risk list grows by tens of thousands; after it, alerts storm.
A change computes the day boundary of the promise-accuracy metric in UTC instead of the destination's local time; the metric for the westernmost region falls 6 points.
A sort centre outage delays a fifth of one day's packages, but the tracking page keeps saying "arriving today" for them until the evening.

templates.title: Multi-account cloud cost and usage analytics
templates.subtopic: restated data, cost allocation, anomaly detection

sections.scenario: A company runs its workloads in {{accounts}} public cloud accounts grouped under one organisation, used by {{teams}} engineering teams. The cloud provider delivers a cost and usage export to object storage: hourly line items per account, resource, service and usage type, with list cost, discounts from commitment purchases (savings plans and reserved capacity), credits, refunds, and the user-defined cost-allocation tags that were active. For the current month the export is rewritten several times a day, and line items can change until the month's invoice is final. That is about {{line_items}} line items a month. About {{untagged}} of spend carries no team tag. Finance wants monthly chargeback per team that matches the invoice to the cent; engineers want daily cost per service and an alert within {{alert_within}} when their spend jumps.
sections.problem: Design the cost analytics platform: ingestion of export files that are rewritten rather than appended; a cost model that allocates shared and untagged spend, spreads commitment purchases over the period they cover, and handles credits and refunds; serving for finance and engineers; spend anomaly detection; and the month-end close that ties to the invoice.
sections.constraints: Monthly totals per account must equal the invoice exactly. Accounts move between teams during the month after reorganisations, and chargeback must follow the move from its effective date. Engineers see their own teams' resource-level detail; organisation-wide views are aggregated. The platform's own compute spend must stay small relative to what it measures.
sections.assumptions: All account counts, volumes and percentages are hypothetical. The export's columns are documented by the provider and change occasionally; files for a month are delivered as a set with a manifest that identifies the version.
sections.criteria: Version-aware ingestion with atomic month swaps and manifest validation; layered model (raw, normalised cost, allocated) with amortised commitments, credits and refunds; a versioned, finance-owned allocation policy for shared and untagged spend with effective-dated account ownership; reconciliation to the invoice at close; anomaly detection that separates scheduled charges from runaway usage and uses a faster signal than the export where needed; access scoped by team; costed processing; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: Do we load every new version of the month's files?
clarifications.a: Every version supersedes the previous one for that month; you decide how much of it you reprocess.

clarifications.q: How is a commitment purchased up front shown?
clarifications.a: As a fee in the month of purchase; the export also carries amortised cost columns that spread it. Finance wants amortised cost for chargeback.

clarifications.q: Who decides how untagged spend is allocated?
clarifications.a: Finance owns the policy; you propose one.

clarifications.q: How fresh is the export?
clarifications.a: Hours behind usage, not minutes.

clarifications.q: Are there shared costs beyond untagged ones?
clarifications.a: Yes: shared clusters, networking, support charges, and data transfer between accounts.

hints: A rewritten file is a new version of the truth for that month, not new rows. Load by version and swap atomically.
Keep three layers apart: raw line items as delivered, a normalised cost fact with amortised and unblended costs, and allocated cost per team under a versioned allocation policy.
The export cannot see a spike faster than it is delivered. Decide what else the alerting can use.
followups: A new version of this month's export arrives while yesterday's dashboards are being served. Walk through loading it so no one ever sees a half-loaded or doubled month.
How do you allocate the shared cluster's cost to the teams that run on it, and how do you explain the result to a team that disputes it?
An account moves from one team to another on the 14th. How is the month split, and what happens if the move is recorded a week late?
How do you detect a spend anomaly within {{alert_within}} without paging forty teams every time a commitment is purchased or a credit lands?
At month close the platform's total differs from the invoice by a small amount for three accounts. How do you find the cause?

rules.ask: The provider rewrites the whole month several times a day. What happens to totals if you append each delivery?
A third of spend is untagged, and tags were added to resources halfway through the month. How does that spend reach a team, and can a team game it?
A team's workload is covered by a commitment the organisation bought. Which cost does the team see, and does it add up to the invoice?
Spend is spiky by nature: month-start fees, weekend batch jobs, credits. How does your detector tell a runaway job from a scheduled one?
The export is hours behind usage. Where does a near-real-time signal come from, and how does it reconcile with the export later?

incidents: A new version of the month's export lands while the loader is midway through the previous one; for two hours dashboards show some accounts' month-to-date cost doubled.
A reorganisation moves 120 of the {{accounts}} accounts to new teams on the 14th, but the mapping is updated on the 21st; finance's draft chargeback assigns the whole month to the old teams.
The organisation buys a large commitment on the 1st. The up-front fee appears as one line item, and the anomaly detector pages dozens of the {{teams}} teams.
A runaway job in one account spends eight times its normal daily cost over a weekend; the alert fires 30 hours after it started, longer than the {{alert_within}} target.

templates.title: Point-in-time feature platform for demand-forecast backtests
templates.subtopic: bitemporal features, point-in-time joins, training–serving parity

sections.scenario: A retailer forecasts weekly demand for {{series}} item-and-region series, {{horizon_weeks}} weeks ahead, and the forecast drives what is bought and where it is placed. Models use about {{features}} features: past sales, prices, planned and actual promotions, product page views, out-of-stock flags (sales are zero when nothing could be sold, which is not the same as zero demand), item attributes and holidays. Many sources are corrected after the fact: returns adjust sales, prices are fixed, promotion calendars are edited weeks after planning. Forecasters test every model change with a backtest that replays {{backtest_years}} years of weekly forecast dates, and the result decides whether it ships.
sections.problem: Design the feature platform: how features are stored with both the time they describe and the time they became known; how training sets and backtests are built with point-in-time joins so each forecast date sees only what was known then; how the weekly production run gets exactly the same feature definitions; how corrections and backfills are handled; and how lineage, cost and freshness are managed.
sections.constraints: A backtest that uses information unavailable on the forecast date is invalid, however good it looks. Production features for every series must be ready by 06:00 on the run day. A feature definition change must not silently change past backtest results. Storage and compute grow with series × features × history; say what that costs.
sections.assumptions: All counts, sizes and timings are hypothetical. Source systems publish changes with an event time; some only publish full daily snapshots.
sections.criteria: Bitemporal storage with valid and knowledge times; point-in-time joins that are correct and laid out to be cheap; backfills with deliberate knowledge times; versioned feature definitions shared by training, backtests and production; explicit handling of censored demand; reproducible backtest manifests; skew-aware joins and precomputation with a costed storage plan; parity checks between production and backtest features; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: Do we keep every correction, or only the latest value?
clarifications.a: That is the core of your design. Say what you keep and for how long.

clarifications.q: How are promotions known in advance?
clarifications.a: Planned promotions are entered weeks ahead and edited; what actually ran is known afterwards. Both are features.

clarifications.q: Are features computed per series, or shared?
clarifications.a: Both. Item attributes are shared across regions; sales are per series.

clarifications.q: How often do forecasters run backtests?
clarifications.a: Dozens a week, each over thousands of forecast dates for a sample or all series.

clarifications.q: Who defines features?
clarifications.a: Forecasting scientists, in code reviewed by the platform team.

hints: Give every feature value two times: valid time (the week it describes) and knowledge time (when the platform learned it). A point-in-time join filters on knowledge time ≤ forecast date and takes the latest value.
A backfill that loads history today must say when that history would have been known, or it is invisible to every backtest.
Define each feature once, as code with a version, and run the same code for training, backtests and production.
followups: Write the point-in-time join for one feature and one forecast date. What index or layout makes it cheap across {{series}} series?
Out-of-stock weeks make observed sales lower than demand. Where in the platform is that handled, and what does the model see?
A scientist changes the definition of a feature. How do old backtests stay reproducible while new ones use the new definition?
The full point-in-time join over {{backtest_years}} years is too slow and too expensive to run dozens of times a week. What do you precompute, and what does that cost in storage?
How would you detect that production features and backtest features for the same date differ?

rules.ask: The price for last March was corrected yesterday. If you keep only the latest snapshot, what does a backtest for last March see?
How do you set knowledge time for a source that only sends full daily snapshots without saying what changed?
The production forecast is a weekly batch. What does an online store buy you here, and what does it cost?
Your backfill is loaded today. Which knowledge time do you give two years of history, and what does each choice do to backtests?
Best-selling items have far more rows than the long tail. What happens to that join's partitions, and how do you fix it?

incidents: A new model beats production by 18% in backtest and loses to it in its first month live. The cause: its promotion feature read the final promotion calendar, including promotions added after each forecast date.
A price source is backfilled for two years with knowledge time set to today. Every backtest since then is missing price for the whole history, and two model changes were approved on those runs.
The weekly production feature build misses 06:00 by 9 hours: the point-in-time join over {{series}} series is skewed on a few thousand best-selling items.

Out-of-stock flags for one region were missing for three weeks; the model read zero sales as zero demand, and the next {{horizon_weeks}}-week forecast for hundreds of items in that region dropped sharply.

templates.title: Multi-tenant metrics ingestion and alarm evaluation for a cloud monitoring service
templates.subtopic: ingestion quotas, rollups, alarm evaluation, cell isolation

sections.scenario: A public cloud offers a managed metrics service in each of its regions. About {{tenants}} customer accounts publish datapoints from their resources and applications: a namespace, a metric name, a few dimensions as name and value pairs, a timestamp and a value. A region receives about {{datapoints}} datapoints per second. Customers graph metrics and create alarms: an alarm evaluates a statistic (average, maximum, a percentile) over a period as short as {{shortest_period}}, goes into alarm when M of the last N periods breach a threshold, lets the customer choose how missing data is treated, and triggers actions such as notifications or scaling. A region holds about {{alarms}} alarms.
sections.problem: Design the service for one region: the ingestion front door with per-tenant limits, storage for recent high-resolution data and for longer-term rollups at coarser resolution, the query path for graphs, and the alarm evaluator, which must evaluate every alarm on schedule. Say how one tenant cannot hurt another, how the region is divided so a failure affects only part of it, and how late datapoints are handled.
sections.constraints: Each region is independent; nothing in one region may depend on another. An alarm must be evaluated within seconds of the end of its period plus a fixed allowance for late data. Graph queries over the last three hours p99 under 1 second. Customers pay per metric and per alarm, so counts must be exact. A datapoint's identity is tenant, namespace, metric name, dimensions and timestamp.
sections.assumptions: All rates, counts and periods are hypothetical. Customers' agents and resources publish with their own clocks and retry on failure.
sections.criteria: Cell-based isolation with tenant placement; per-tenant rate and series-count limits enforced at the front door; idempotent ingestion keyed by datapoint identity; statistic sets with mergeable sketches; tiered rollups with retention; an evaluator scheduled by period with a lateness allowance, missing-data semantics applied correctly and action firing on state change only; protection against cascading false alarms during the service's own degradation; timestamp validation; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: Can a datapoint arrive after its period was evaluated?
clarifications.a: Yes, sometimes minutes later. The customer's missing-data choice decides how an empty period counts.

clarifications.q: Is a new combination of dimensions a new metric?
clarifications.a: Yes. Each unique combination is a separate time series and is billed as a metric.

clarifications.q: What resolution must be kept, and for how long?
clarifications.a: High resolution for hours to days, then coarser rollups for longer; you choose the tiers and say what queries lose.

clarifications.q: Do alarm actions need exactly-once delivery?
clarifications.a: An action fires on a state change; firing it twice for one change is a defect customers notice.

hints: Partition the region into cells, each holding a subset of tenants end to end (ingestion, storage, evaluation), so a bad cell or a bad tenant affects a bounded share of customers.
Pre-aggregate at ingestion into per-series, per-period statistic sets (count, sum, min, max and a mergeable sketch for percentiles) rather than storing and rescanning raw points.
Alarm evaluation is a scheduling problem: millions of small jobs due at period boundaries. Avoid making them all read storage at the same second.
followups: How does ingestion enforce per-tenant limits on datapoints and on new series without slowing well-behaved tenants?
Walk through evaluating one alarm with a {{shortest_period}} period and "3 of 5" datapoints: when does it run, what does it read, and what if the last period's data is late?
How do you compute a p99 statistic for a period when datapoints for one series arrive at several ingestion hosts?
How do you move a very large tenant from one cell to another without missing an evaluation or firing a duplicate action?
What do customers see during a partial outage of the evaluator, and how do you decide whether to evaluate late or skip?

rules.ask: How is that log partitioned, and what happens to a partition when one tenant suddenly publishes a hundred times its usual rate?
Most alarms have one-minute periods, so tens of millions of evaluations are due at the top of each minute. How do you spread that load without making alarms late?
At {{datapoints}} per second, what does storing every raw point cost, and which queries actually need it?
Can the evaluator average per-host p99 values for one period? If not, what do the hosts send?
An agent retries a batch that was already accepted. How is the datapoint not counted twice in the sum statistic?

incidents: A tenant deploys code that adds a request-id dimension to one metric; it creates millions of new series an hour, and its cell's ingestion latency rises for every tenant on it.
Ingestion in one cell falls 3 minutes behind. Alarms that treat missing data as breaching fire for thousands of customers and trigger scale-out actions they did not need.

During a large regional event, datapoints from {{tenants}} customers spike together and graph queries triple; the evaluator falls behind and alarms with a {{shortest_period}} period are evaluated late.
One customer's agents publish datapoints timestamped two hours in the future, and that customer's dashboards and alarms behave strangely.

templates.title: Delivery promises broken by stale carrier capacity data
templates.subtopic: data correctness, customer promises, cross-team response

cause: a pipeline that kept republishing the last good capacity file after its source stopped updating
a schema change upstream that turned missing capacity values into zeros the loader read as unlimited
a backfill that overwrote this week's capacity with last year's holiday figures

sections.scenario: Your team owns the pipeline that feeds daily delivery-station and carrier capacity into the service that sets the delivery date shown at checkout. For {{hours}} hours during a busy shopping weekend, the capacity that checkout read was wrong; the cause was {{cause}}. Checkout promised dates the network could not meet, and about {{orders}} orders now carry promises that will be missed. Customers have started contacting support, the operations teams are moving volume between stations by hand, and you are the most senior engineer on the team.
sections.problem: Tell me how you would lead the response in the first hour, the first day and the following weeks. Cover stopping new bad promises, working out exactly which orders are affected and by how much, what customers are told and when, how you work with the operations, checkout and customer-service teams, and how you prevent a repeat. Then tell me about a real incident where data you owned caused customer-visible harm (situation, your actions, measurable result), or say that you have not and reason through how you would.
sections.constraints: You do not own the checkout service, the operations teams or customer messaging. Promised dates already shown to customers cannot be silently changed. Operations can add some capacity, but not enough to save every order.
sections.assumptions: The situation and figures are hypothetical.
sections.criteria: Contains first with an explicit trade-off (conservative fallback, pinning to last verified data, regional scoping); precise definition and count of affected orders reconciled with operations; works through owners it does not control with clear facts and decision rights; customer communication that is timely and honest without over-alarming; prevention that tests content (distribution shifts, unchanged files, zero or unlimited values) with an owner and threshold; real example with measurable evidence and personal contribution, or honestly hypothetical.

clarifications.q: Is the bad data still flowing when you are paged?
clarifications.a: You do not know yet. The alert is from operations: one station's volume for tomorrow is far above its capacity.

clarifications.q: Can checkout fall back to something safer?
clarifications.a: It has a conservative default capacity setting, but turning it on lengthens promises for every customer.

clarifications.q: Who decides what customers are told?
clarifications.a: Customer-service and checkout leaders, using your numbers.

clarifications.q: Did any check exist on the capacity feed?
clarifications.a: Row counts and a freshness timestamp on the file, both of which passed.

hints: Contain first: what is the fastest switch that stops new wrong promises, and what does it cost?
The affected list is a join between orders, their promised dates and the capacity they consumed. Define "affected" before you count.
The checks that passed tell you what the next check must measure: content, not just arrival.
followups: Turning on the conservative capacity default lengthens promises for every customer, including those in regions the bug did not touch. Do you turn it on? Who decides?
Operations can save some orders by moving volume. How do you help them choose which ones?
Your list of affected orders is 15% larger than operations' estimate. How do you resolve the difference before customers are contacted?
What check would have caught this failure within an hour of it starting? Name the signal, the threshold and the owner.
In your real example, what did you personally decide, and what would you do differently?

rules.ask: Rolling back the pipeline stops new bad data, but checkout has cached the capacity it already read. What else must happen before promises are right again?
Some of those orders will still arrive on time after operations moves volume. How many customers would you alarm unnecessarily, and does that matter?
Name one change from the review that actually shipped, and how you checked it would catch this exact failure.
What did you personally decide or do?
The existing checks passed. What property of the data do your new checks measure that the old ones did not?

templates.title: One shared order-events table, many writers, no contracts
templates.subtopic: data contracts, platform adoption

sections.scenario: A shared table of marketplace order events (placed, item cancelled, shipped, returned, refunded) is written by {{writers}} teams' services and read by {{consumers}}, among many others. Nobody owns its schema. A team renames a field, changes a status value, or starts emitting events for a new order type, and something downstream breaks; that has happened {{breaks}} times in the last quarter, each found days later by a consumer. You lead the data platform team, which runs the table's infrastructure but does not manage any of the writing teams.
sections.problem: How would you fix this? Cover how you establish what is actually written and read, what you propose (data contracts, ownership, validation, versioning or something else), how you get teams you do not manage to adopt it while they have their own roadmaps, how you roll it out without breaking the consumers you are trying to protect, and how you know it worked. Then describe a real change you drove across teams that did not report to you, with its outcome, or say that you have not and reason it through.
sections.constraints: You cannot stop the writing teams from shipping. The table cannot be frozen; new order types are launched every quarter. Your team has two engineers for this.
sections.assumptions: The situation and figures are hypothetical.
sections.criteria: Evidence first (field-level usage, cost of each break); a proposal sized to two engineers (contracts per event type, ownership, compatibility rules, checks in the writer's pipeline, versioned changes); adoption through value to writers and a pilot with the most painful sources; a rollout in warn-then-block stages that protects consumers; clear decision rights for blocked deploys; measures of success (breaks, time to detect, adoption); real example of cross-team influence with a measured outcome and personal contribution, or honestly hypothetical.

clarifications.q: Does leadership support this?
clarifications.a: They agree it is a problem; they have not given you any authority over the writing teams.

clarifications.q: Is there any schema documentation?
clarifications.a: A wiki page, last edited a year ago.

clarifications.q: Do consumers know which fields they use?
clarifications.a: Roughly. Nobody has measured it.

clarifications.q: Do writing teams know they break consumers?
clarifications.a: Most learn about it from an angry message days later.

hints: Measure before you propose: which fields are read, by whom, and what each break cost.
The cheapest adoption path is one that makes the writing team's life easier, not just the consumer's.
Start where breaks hurt most and prove the approach on two or three writers before asking all of them.
followups: What does a contract for one event type contain, and where is it enforced: in the writer's build, at publish time, or at the table?
The team that caused the most breaks says they have no time this quarter. What do you do?
A contract check blocks a writing team's deploy on launch day. Who decides whether it ships?
Six months in, how do you know this worked, and what would make you change course?
In your real example, who resisted, why, and what changed their mind?

rules.ask: You have no authority over the writing teams. Who enforces it, and what happens the first time a team ignores it?
The last documentation went stale within a year. What keeps yours true?
What does a writing team have to do differently on day one, and how long does it take them?
What would you put in front of leadership, and what do you ask them to decide?

templates.title: A multi-year compute commitment the forecast cannot yet justify
templates.subtopic: cloud commitments, finance partnership

uncertainty: a planned migration of the batch platform to a different compute type
a forecasting model rewrite that may halve or double training compute
a new marketplace region whose demand is unknown

sections.scenario: Your data platform spends about {{spend}} on cloud compute at on-demand prices. Finance proposes buying a {{term}} commitment covering most of today's usage, which would cut that cost by about {{discount}} on what it covers. You own the platform's architecture, and the decision needs your recommendation. The difficulty is {{uncertainty}}, so you do not know what the platform will use in a year.
sections.problem: How would you reach and present a recommendation? Cover the data you gather about current and future usage, how you size the commitment (all, some or none), how you weigh the saving against the risk of paying for capacity you no longer use, how the commitment interacts with the architecture choices ahead, and how you keep the decision under review. Then tell me about a real decision where you traded a cost saving against flexibility, with its outcome, or say that you have not and reason it through.
sections.constraints: The commitment cannot be cancelled once bought. Finance needs an answer this month. The engineering roadmap cannot be held hostage to the commitment.
sections.assumptions: The situation and figures are hypothetical. The commitment applies to a flexible family of compute rather than a single instance type unless you choose otherwise.
sections.criteria: Usage data at hourly grain separated into base, peak and uncertain components; commitment sized to the base that survives every scenario, layered over time; break-even arithmetic stated (a discount d breaks even at a utilisation of 1 − d); risk framed for finance in money terms with scenarios; architecture decisions kept free where flexibility matters; review cadence with triggers; real example with numbers and personal contribution, or honestly hypothetical.

clarifications.q: Is usage steady?
clarifications.a: There is a steady base, a nightly batch peak, and month-end spikes.

clarifications.q: Can commitments be layered?
clarifications.a: Yes. You can buy part now and more later.

clarifications.q: Who owns the decision?
clarifications.a: Finance signs; your recommendation carries the technical risk.

clarifications.q: How confident is the usage forecast?
clarifications.a: That is for you to establish.

hints: Separate the base that will exist in every plausible future from the usage that depends on the uncertain change.
Compute the break-even: how much of the committed usage can disappear before the commitment costs more than on-demand?
Commitment flexibility (family-level versus instance-level) has a price; compare it with the architecture risk.
followups: Show me how you would size the commitment from the last six months of hourly usage. Which percentile of usage do you commit to, and why?
What is the break-even utilisation at a {{discount}} discount, and what does that tell you?
Six months after the purchase, usage covered by the commitment falls 40%. What happens to the bill, and what could you have done at purchase time?
A year later, an engineer proposes moving a large workload to a cheaper compute type that the commitment does not cover. How do you decide?
In your real example, what did the decision cost or save, measured how?

rules.ask: The usage you commit to includes the nightly peak and the month-end spikes. How many hours a month is that capacity unused?
You are leaving a {{discount}} discount on the table for the steady base that will exist anyway. How do you justify that to finance?
How wrong was the last usage forecast for this platform, and how does that error shape your recommendation?
Which of the platform's workloads tolerate interruption, and how much of the cost do they represent?

templates.title: A peer's reservation design that you believe can oversell
templates.subtopic: design review, evidence, escalation

peer: a principal engineer from the checkout team
a respected senior engineer on your own team
the engineer who built the current reservation service
benefit: a third of the reservation service's hardware cost saved
the deal-day hot-key problem gone without re-sharding

sections.scenario: Ahead of the next big sale, {{peer}} proposes replacing the inventory reservation path with in-memory counters per region that are reconciled with the inventory ledger every few seconds. The design review document promises {{benefit}}. You have read it closely and believe that under a burst of orders for one deal item, two regions can each sell the last units before reconciliation runs, so the deal can oversell. The proposal is popular, the design review is in a week, and building would start in {{weeks}} weeks.
sections.problem: What do you do? Cover how you check that your concern is real before you raise it, how you raise it with the author, how you bring evidence to the review, what you propose instead (or as a change to the design), how a decision gets made if you and the author still disagree, and what you do once it is made, whichever way it goes. Then tell me about a real time you disagreed with a peer's technical design, with what happened, or say that you have not and reason it through.
sections.constraints: You are not the author's manager, and the author is at least as senior as you. The sale date does not move. Overselling a deal means cancelling orders customers were told were confirmed.
sections.assumptions: The situation and figures are hypothetical.
sections.criteria: Verifies the concern first and makes it concrete (an event sequence, a simulation, a quantified oversell rate at the expected load); raises it early and privately, as a question, with respect for the author; brings evidence to the review and proposes design changes that keep most of the benefit (for example exact reservations for capped deal items only, per-region allotments that cannot exceed the cap, or an exact final check at order confirmation); respects decision rights and escalates fairly if needed; commits fully once decided while making the residual risk visible and monitored; real example with what changed and personal contribution, or honestly hypothetical.

clarifications.q: Has anyone else raised the concern?
clarifications.a: Not in writing. One engineer mentioned "consistency" in a comment without detail.

clarifications.q: Is the benefit real?
clarifications.a: The latency or cost benefit is plausible; the author has a benchmark.

clarifications.q: Who decides after the review?
clarifications.a: The owning team's lead, with the review's input; escalation goes to the director over both teams.

clarifications.q: Can the design be changed rather than rejected?
clarifications.a: Yes, and the author would rather change it than lose it.

hints: Turn the concern into something testable: a sequence of events, or a small simulation, that oversells.
Raise it with the author first, privately and early, as a question about the design rather than a verdict on it.
Look for a design that keeps most of the benefit and removes the risk; the choice is rarely all or nothing.
followups: How would you demonstrate the oversell risk concretely, and how likely is it at the deal's expected order rate?
The author agrees there is a window for overselling but says it is small enough to accept. How do you decide together how small is small enough?
What changes to the design would keep most of the promised benefit without the risk?
The decision goes the author's way. What do you do in the {{weeks}} weeks before building starts, and on the day of the sale?
In your real example, what evidence moved the decision, and what did the disagreement do to the working relationship?

rules.ask: What do you put in front of the director, and how do you show the author's case as fairly as your own?
You are not the decider. What happens if the owning team's lead approves it anyway?
Your test shows an oversell rate of one in a million orders. Is that acceptable? Who should say so?
Which part of the benefit does your hybrid give up, and does the author agree it is worth it?
What did you personally do or say, and when?

templates.title: Proving the order pipeline is ready for peak season
templates.subtopic: load testing, risk, go/no-go across teams

last_year: order events lagged three hours behind and seller reports were late for two days
a downstream returns service throttled and order confirmations were delayed for forty minutes
nothing failed, but only because a manual throttle was applied by one engineer at 2 a.m.

sections.scenario: A large shopping event is {{weeks}} weeks away. Your team owns the order-event pipeline that carries placed, cancelled, shipped and returned order events from checkout to {{dependencies}} downstream systems: fulfilment, payments, seller reports, analytics, forecasting and others owned by other teams. Peak order rate is expected at {{multiplier}} a normal day. Last year, {{last_year}}. Leadership has asked you to lead readiness for the pipeline and to make a go or no-go call on the planned changes your team wants to ship before the event.
sections.problem: How would you lead it? Cover how you find the limits of your pipeline and its dependencies, how you test them without harming production, what you change and what you freeze, how you get the other teams to take part, what is decided in advance for the day itself (alarms, levers, who is on call), and how you would decide whether a planned change ships. Then tell me about a real high-stakes launch or peak event you prepared for, with what happened, or say that you have not and reason it through.
sections.constraints: You do not own the downstream systems. Load tests in production need the other teams' agreement. Your team also has committed feature work.
sections.assumptions: The situation and figures are hypothetical.
sections.criteria: Readiness driven by evidence (capacity model per stage and dependency, end-to-end load tests at and beyond the expected peak with synthetic traffic that cannot become real orders); fixes prioritised by the first limit hit; dependencies brought in with clear asks and owners; levers, alarms, on-call and escalation decided and rehearsed before the day; change decisions based on value, risk and reversibility, with a stricter freeze where warranted; last year's failure explicitly addressed; real example with what happened and personal contribution, or honestly hypothetical.

clarifications.q: Has the pipeline been load-tested before?
clarifications.a: Last year, at a lower rate, and only up to its own boundary.

clarifications.q: Can traffic be shaped on the day?
clarifications.a: Some consumers can be slowed or paused; checkout itself cannot be.

clarifications.q: Who makes the final go/no-go on the event's changes?
clarifications.a: You, for your pipeline, with an escalation path to the event's overall leader.

clarifications.q: Is there a change freeze?
clarifications.a: A general one starts one week before the event; you can set a stricter one.

hints: Find the first thing that breaks at {{multiplier}}, then the second. Test the whole chain, not only your part.
Decide the levers before the day: which consumers can be slowed, what is shed first, and who may pull each lever.
A planned change ships only if its value before the event exceeds its risk, and it can be turned off in minutes.
followups: Walk me through the load test plan: what traffic, where, at what rate, and how you protect real customers during it.
A downstream team says they cannot take part in testing before the event. What do you do?
Your test shows the pipeline holds at {{multiplier}}, but one consumer falls behind at half that. What do you change, and who owns it?
Your team wants to ship a new partitioning scheme three weeks before the event because it fixes last year's lag. Go or no-go, and on what evidence?
In your real example, what did you get wrong in preparation, and what did you change afterwards?

rules.ask: Your test traffic flows into the payments and fulfilment systems downstream. How do you keep it from becoming real orders or real charges?
The freeze blocks a fix for a bug you find in week two of testing. How do you decide whether the fix goes out?
Which part of the pipeline cannot scale by adding machines, such as a partition count or a downstream limit, and what is your plan for it?
Who has rehearsed that runbook under load, and what did the rehearsal change?
Which call did you personally make, and what did it cost?
